items.topic: Physical nature and composition of natural gas
items.definition: Natural gas is a nonrenewable fossil fuel that exists as a colorless, odorless gas mixture at room temperature, used mainly for heating and power generation.
items.core_idea: Natural gas is mostly methane but can carry varying amounts of ethane, propane, butane, and non-hydrocarbon gases like nitrogen and CO2, so its composition — and therefore its heat content per unit volume — is not fixed.
key_points: Primary component is methane (CH4); commonly present alongside ethane (C2H6), propane (C3H8), and butane (C4H10)
'Dry' gas is nearly pure methane; 'wet' gas carries significant amounts of the heavier hydrocarbons
Can also contain non-hydrocarbon gases such as nitrogen and carbon dioxide
Because composition varies, it is traded in heat-energy units (Btu, Joules) rather than volume units like cubic feet
relationships: Composition variability is the reason gas is priced/traded by energy content rather than volume
trading_implications: Traders must think in energy-content terms (Btu/MMBtu) rather than raw volume when comparing gas across sources of differing composition
common_misunderstandings: Assuming natural gas is a pure, uniform substance (pure methane) rather than a variable hydrocarbon mixture
related_topics: Energy unit conversions (Btu, MMBtu, Bcf, therm)

items.definition: Natural gas relies on an extensive, capital-intensive network of pipelines to move gas from producing regions to consumers, and this sunk infrastructure creates structural, durable demand.
items.core_idea: Once pipeline networks and household/utility hookups are built, replacing them with infrastructure for a different fuel is prohibitively expensive, which locks in consumers as a 'captive audience' and cements natural gas's long-term role in heating and power.
key_points: Transcontinental pipelines move gas between regions; local pipelines handle final delivery to consumers within a limited area
A low-price period in the 1970s-1980s spurred a natural gas infrastructure construction boom
Demand growth later pushed prices up, but the already-built infrastructure kept consumers reliant on gas
Once pipelines exist, transportation costs for gas become small relative to other fuels
Nearly all U.S. fossil-fuel power plants built since 1990 can burn natural gas, tying electricity prices closely to gas prices
relationships: Sunk pipeline/appliance infrastructure -> inelastic, captive residential and power-generation demand
Natural gas price levels are structurally linked to electricity prices because of the prevalence of gas-capable power plants
trading_implications: Structural, infrastructure-driven demand makes natural gas consumption relatively inelastic in the short-to-medium term, which matters for weather-driven demand spikes
Strong gas-to-power linkage means gas price moves are a key driver of electricity price moves
common_misunderstandings: Believing natural gas is still 'extremely cheap' as it was decades ago; the author notes this is no longer true despite that reputation persisting
related_topics: Natural gas as a fuel for power generation

items.topic: Natural gas pricing conventions and price behavior
items.definition: Natural gas is typically priced as a differential (spread) to a benchmark index rather than as an outright price, and its spot and futures prices behave differently from typical financial/commodity assets.
items.core_idea: In North America the benchmark reference point is Henry Hub, a major Gulf Coast pipeline interconnection; spot prices are strongly weather-driven, and futures prices move in cyclical patterns rather than tracking spot through a simple cost-of-carry relationship.
key_points: Gas prices are quoted as a spread relative to an index, with Henry Hub as the primary North American benchmark
Spot prices are heavily influenced by weather
Futures prices exhibit cyclicality
Unlike stocks, bonds, or gold, natural gas futures prices are not tied to spot prices via a standard cost-of-carry relationship
relationships: Henry Hub acts as the reference point that regional/local gas prices are quoted against as a basis/spread
trading_implications: Cost-of-carry / storage-arbitrage models used for financial assets do not reliably price natural gas futures relative to spot
Weather forecasts are a primary input for anticipating natural gas spot price moves
common_misunderstandings: Assuming natural gas futures can be priced off spot plus a standard carrying-cost model, the way futures are priced for stocks, bonds, or gold

items.topic: Natural gas energy-content units and conversions
items.definition: Standard approximate conversions used to express natural gas quantities in heat-energy terms rather than volume, since composition (and thus energy content per volume) varies.
items.core_idea: Dry natural gas has roughly a fixed Btu content per cubic foot, which lets volume-based figures (like Bcf) be translated into energy-based figures (like MMBtu), and consumer billing uses a smaller derived unit, the therm.
key_points: These are approximate figures for dry (nearly pure methane) gas specifically — wet gas with heavier hydrocarbons would have different energy content per volume
A therm is the standard consumer billing unit, equal to one-tenth of an MMBtu

formulas.name: Dry gas heat content
formulas.formula: 1 cubic foot of dry natural gas ≈ 1,000 Btu

variables.Btu: British Thermal Unit, a unit of heat energy
variables.cubic foot: unit of gas volume at standard conditions

variables.Bcf: billion cubic feet of natural gas

variables.therm: standard consumer natural gas billing unit

relationships: These conversions link the volume-based units used in production/transport (Bcf) to the energy-based units used in trading (MMBtu) and retail billing (therms)
trading_implications: Wholesale gas trading and consumer billing use different unit conventions (MMBtu vs. therms), so conversion is needed when comparing prices across the value chain
common_misunderstandings: Treating natural gas volumes (e.g., cubic feet) as directly comparable across different gas streams without accounting for varying Btu content per unit volume

items.topic: Why natural gas is transported by pipeline rather than pressurized containers
items.definition: Methane's low energy density per unit volume, relative to heavier hydrocarbons, makes pipeline transport the practical choice over pressurized container shipping.
items.core_idea: Because methane holds relatively little heat energy per unit of volume compared to longer-chain hydrocarbons like propane or butane, moving it in pressurized metal containers would require impractically large containers, so pipelines are used instead.
key_points: Propane and butane contain enough energy density to be practically shipped in pressurized metal containers
Methane requires a much larger container to hold an equivalent amount of heat energy, making container transport impractical at scale
Pipelines solve this by allowing continuous transport without needing to contain large volumes under pressure in discrete vessels
relationships: Low energy density of methane -> reliance on pipeline infrastructure rather than tanker/cylinder transport
trading_implications: Regions without pipeline access to a given supply source face a structurally different (and often costlier) transport option: liquefaction/LNG shipping
common_misunderstandings: Assuming natural gas could be economically shipped in pressurized tanks the way propane or butane are
related_topics: LNG as an alternative transport method

items.definition: LNG is natural gas that has been supercooled into liquid form to increase its energy density for transport or storage, typically converted back to gas before reaching end consumers.
items.core_idea: Liquefaction (cooling gas to about −263°F) makes natural gas dense enough to transport economically over long ocean distances where pipelines aren't feasible, and it can also serve as a storage method, but it is generally regasified before delivery since consumers lack equipment to handle supercooled liquid.
key_points: Liquefaction requires cooling natural gas to approximately −263°F
Liquids are much denser than gases, so LNG holds substantially more heat energy per unit volume than gaseous natural gas
LNG's main use is long-distance ocean transport where pipeline construction is impractical; it is also sometimes used for storage
Natural gas is almost always converted back to gas form before final delivery through local distribution pipelines
relationships: Liquefaction trades off increased energy density against the cost/complexity of supercooling and specialized handling equipment
trading_implications: LNG shipping enables natural gas trade between regions not connected by pipeline (e.g., intercontinental trade), effectively globalizing what is otherwise a regionally-bound commodity
common_misunderstandings: Assuming LNG is delivered to end consumers in liquid form; in practice it is regasified before local distribution

items.topic: Energy density comparison: gasoline vs. natural gas
items.definition: A worked comparison of storage volume needed for equivalent heat energy from gasoline versus natural gas in various forms (atmospheric, compressed, liquefied).
items.core_idea: Gasoline is far more energy-dense by volume than natural gas at atmospheric pressure, and even substantial compression or liquefaction does not fully close that gap.
key_points: One gallon of gasoline contains about 124,000 Btu and occupies about 0.13 cubic feet
The same amount of energy in natural gas at standard atmospheric pressure requires about 100 cubic feet of storage

At about 250 times atmospheric pressure (roughly comparable to scuba tank compression levels of 200-300x), natural gas still needs about three times the storage volume of gasoline, plus a heavy pressurized cylinder
As supercooled liquid (LNG), natural gas holds about two-thirds the energy per volume of gasoline
relationships: Illustrates numerically why natural gas transport/storage logistics (pipeline, compression, or liquefaction) differ fundamentally from liquid fuels like gasoline
trading_implications: Explains why natural gas vehicles/storage face practical volume/weight penalties compared to liquid fuels, relevant to any gas-as-transport-fuel economics
common_misunderstandings: Assuming compression alone (e.g., to scuba-tank-like pressures) brings natural gas storage density close to gasoline; the source shows it still needs roughly 3x the volume even at ~250x atmospheric pressure

items.topic: Natural gas value chain and market participants
items.definition: The natural gas business is divided into distinct physical roles from extraction to final delivery, plus a separate financial/trading function.
items.core_idea: Natural gas moves through exploration, drilling/extraction, processing, transport (pipeline or tanker), storage, and local distribution, with most physical companies specializing in only one or two of these stages; trading itself is a distinct function handled by natural gas marketers.
key_points: Exploration companies locate underground natural gas reserves
Drilling companies extract gas and move it to processing facilities
Processing plants remove impurities and separate the raw gas into component hydrocarbons, yielding dry gas (methane)
Dry gas is transported to consuming regions via interstate pipeline or tanker ship, then stored until needed
Local distribution pipelines make final delivery to the end consumer
Most physical-side companies specialize narrowly because each stage is technically complex
The skills required for physical natural gas operations differ substantially from those needed to trade/speculate on the financial commodity, so trading is handled by natural gas marketers
relationships: Physical value-chain specialization is distinct from and does not overlap with financial trading expertise
trading_implications: Natural gas marketers, not upstream/midstream physical operators, are the relevant counterparties/participants for financial trading and speculation in natural gas
common_misunderstandings: Assuming the same companies that extract, process, or transport natural gas are also the primary financial traders of the commodity
